item.content:encoded:
Just one problem with this - the abuse of statistics in the last few lines before the collapsibles. "1 in 8 women will get breast cancer in 2015" is simply untrue, if that was the case there'd be an untreatable epidemic with the better part of 450 million new cases worldwide each year, and within a decade almost the entire female population of Earth would be suffering from some kind of aggressive mammary neoplasm. Around 22 million in the USA alone, or 4.5 million in the UK. It'd be easily the #1 problem facing medical science.

The correct way of expressing it is that 1 in 8 females born in 2015 will suffer the development of breast cancer sometime in their lifetime. It's a brutally common and deadly disease, but even so, the greater majority of women don't suffer it, a decent and increasing proportion of those who do now survive it, and things like heart disease, cancer of other organs, and succumbing to infections with an immune system ravaged by age (or other multifarious symptoms of sheer wear & tear) are still far more likely to do you in.

item.content:encoded:
Damn fine work. Like some others, I thought this was going in a very … unfortunate direction, which was what lent the tension for me to keep reading. The fact that it seemed like he might be doing something awful to cancer patients made it even more tense. The co-mingled relief and sadness I felt at the final reveal was just right for a +1.

And it seems to me like the complaints about it being unrealistic that this guy managed to pull the wool over Foundation's eyes is a case of Reality is Unrealistic. People do this sort of thing all the time and get away with it until they slip up. Embezzlers can go for years without getting caught if they resist the urge to get too greedy.

And corruption exists all over the place, sometimes pretty openly since several corrupt people in the system can cover up for each other. I can certainly see something like that being the case here, especially given why guy was doing what he did. All he needed to do was seek out a small selection of other Foundation researchers who had been affected by cancer to work on the project with him, provide him with resources, or at the very least vouch for him, saying yeah, hey, this is legit. And the D-Class sure aren't going to snitch on him since, y'know, he's trying to cure their cancer. I'd probably keep my lips zipped too under the circumstances.

But aside from all that, I also think folks might not be giving the Foundation enough credit. Sure, the hammer didn't really come down until the doc really truly slipped up, but personally, I read the denial for cross-testing the second SCP object as being the higher ups starting to get suspicious. They didn't know enough to actually stop him, but just maybe they suspected enough to start denying him certain resources. If that was the case, then he simply ended up bringin his downfall upon himself sooner rather than later.

item.content:encoded:
Thanks for reading and pointing some things out. I would love to discuss/get some more input on these points and make the story better:

+ Note From EC-3 Spoiler
- hide

So the biggest challenge of all in writing this story was getting the information across to the reader because I didn’t want Harold to fail because he was dumb. That means the initial document has to be a well written lie with no obvious tell. (Yes, a lot of people familiar with it have noticed that it is mainly the list of breast cancer symptoms with some smudging, but that’s kind of the point.)

Initially, I had the first section as document on its own, then the Evidence, then the Ethics Committee Conversation, and in that iteration, I was mainly told that the first two sections were boring with no story and then section three “revealed the whole story and by that point, we don’t care.”

As a compromise, I added EC-3’s note (since 3’s compiling the investigation) to point out the what of the lie, but not the why, and left the why to be sorted out in section two.

+ Blackboxed SCPs
- hide

So the two blackboxed SCPs are very differently animals.

The second one is a very specific reference to SCP-500. The request email is sent using the format from the 500 article, and the reason it’s blackboxed is two-fold. Out of universe, I didn’t want to crosslink a heritage article willy-nilly. In universe, I actually think people request/try to steal it all the dang time and The Foundation probably redacts a lot of information about 500 nowadays because of it.

The first one? I admit, I didn’t pick one. The first one only exists because I felt that structurally, he shouldn’t jump straight to 500. It also let me slide that “Bodies disposed of.” in there and that made me chuckle.

+ Use of the O5 in the finale?
- hide

I’m confused. I mention them in the Ethics Chair’s dialogue, but they don’t actually feature. Could you elaborate?

(My feeling of this section was aiming towards hitting that cold beauracracy feeling, so to the Ethics Committee, this is just one of several cases in this meeting, and their suggested punishment takes the situation into account, burn in a quick and unattached way. When it comes to the O5s, I assume they are understandably used to haggling with the O5 Council who I imagine meets out harsher punishments usually.)

As I realize I ended every point, I appreciate any input you might have to better these issues.

item.content:encoded:
Oh yeah, I totally agree that Researchers don't work in a vacuum. My imagination is that he had a very small team of research assistants AND he had to submit this proposal to his higher-ups and provide updates on research progress.

However, at least in my head, I think Harold tweaked it enough to get it in the door;

1) The last symptom is full body necrotizing fasciitis; that's a hugely exaggerated combination of the oozing sore symptom and the metastasizing symptom. It makes it sound dangerous.
2) Highly contagious? Cancer isn't contagious at all, so that's weird.
3) Using the absolutely true number that 1 in 8 women will get breast cancer (~12.5%) to sell this as an emergency epidemic situation. If we don't contain this now, we will certainly break secrecy sooner than later.

Coming from an employee who you trust and have no reason to disbelieve, I think this would make a pretty solid case.

Now I will agree that even though I've thought out a lot about how Harold fooled the Foundation and kept his cover-up going, a lot of that didn't make it into the story. Part of that is format challenge, since there's not much about the cover-up that I could find a way to fit within the bounds of the SCP Document, and if his Research Notes flat out said he was lying then he'd be caught. I'm wondering if there are other ways to talk about those situations where his assistant finds something and he has to convince him that it's not an issue, or his bosses have questions and he has to think his way out of them. Sounds like a cool idea for a one man Ocean's Eleven type Tale…

item.title: Author Post
item.content:encoded:
Official Audio Adaptation: https://youtu.be/jSv_EQtohkk

Okay guys, this is my first time writing a story with a personal reason; it actually made it harder for me because I knew what I was trying to say but I had to keep adding on more and more because I wasn't communicating that to the reader.

Also, if we need a skip for Breast Cancer Awareness Month, I got you fam.

Special thanks to

Westrin (for critting it multiple times)
not_a_seagull (for the Draft Forum Crit)
BlazingTrail (for having exceeding faith in the concept and a couple crits)
Doctor Cimmerian (for a crit that cut to the heart of the issue in a thoroughly academic way)
PhamtomGuy (especially for picking the appropriate SCP number)

+ Cliff's Notes to this Skip
- Hide

SCP-2700-EX is breast cancer. Run of the mill, non-anomalous breast cancer.
Harold's wife got breast cancer. He made up the fact that it was contagious and made it sound super scary so the Foundation would research it.
He tried to use an SCP to cure it. It got worse.
He tried to get a cross-test with SCP-500, but was denied.
He tried to steal a pill of SCP-500. It didn't go well.
The Ethics Committee let him off easy.
